SystemVerilog Assertion (SVA) Quick Reference

All temporal operators, system functions, and common patterns at a glance.

⏱️ Temporal Operators
OperatorSyntaxMeaningExample
##Na ##N bExactly N cycles laterreq ##2 ack
##[M:N]a ##[1:5] bBetween M and N cycles laterreq ##[1:5] ack
##[*]a ##[0:$] b0 to infinity cycles (eventually)req ##[0:$] ack
[*N]a[*3]Consecutive repetition: a for exactly N cyclesvalid[*4]
[*M:N]a[*1:5]Consecutive repetition M to N timesbusy[*1:8]
[+]a[+]Consecutive repetition 1 or morevalid[+]
[=N]a[=3]Non-consecutive: a true exactly N timeserr[=2]
[->N]a[->3]Goto: a true N times, last occurrence ends seqack[->1]
throughoutb throughout seqb must hold true throughout seq!rst throughout (req ##[1:5] ack)
withins1 within s2s1 must match within the window of s2(a ##1 b) within (c[*5])
intersects1 intersect s2Both sequences match simultaneously, same start+endseq1 intersect seq2
first_matchfirst_match(seq)Only first match of non-det sequencefirst_match(a ##[1:5] b)
ands1 and s2Both sequences must match, same start pointseq_a and seq_b
ors1 or s2Either sequence must matchseq_a or seq_b
➡️ Implication Operators
OperatorMeaningVacuous Pass?Example
|-> (overlapping)If antecedent matches, consequent starts same cycleYesreq |-> ack
|=> (non-overlapping)If antecedent matches, consequent starts next cycleYesreq |=> ##1 ack
strong()Sequence must actually match (no vacuous pass)Nostrong(a ##1 b)
weak()Like strong but vacuously passes if sequence can't matchYesweak(a ##1 b)
🔧 System Functions
FunctionReturnsNote
$rose(sig)1 when sig transitions 0→1 at clock edgeSamples prev + curr cycle
$fell(sig)1 when sig transitions 1→0 at clock edgeOpposite of $rose
$stable(sig)1 when sig has same value as previous cycle!$changed(sig)
$changed(sig)1 when sig differs from previous cycle!$stable(sig)
$past(sig,N)Value of sig N cycles agoDefault N=1
$onehot(vec)1 if exactly one bit setChecks one-hot encoding
$onehot0(vec)1 if at most one bit set (includes all-zero)Allows zero
$countones(vec)Count of '1' bits in vectorReturns int
$isunknown(vec)1 if any bit is X or ZChecks X-propagation
$assertoff(lvl,hier)Disable assertions in hierarchyUse 0 = disable all
$asserton(lvl,hier)Re-enable assertionsPairs with $assertoff
📋 SVA Template
property p_name;
  @(posedge clk) disable iff (rst)
  antecedent_seq |-> ##[N:M] consequent_expr;
endproperty
assert property(p_name) else `uvm_error("SVA","...");
cover property(p_name);

SDC / Timing Constraint Quick Reference

Most-used Synopsys Design Constraints commands with syntax and key options.

⏰ Clock Definitions
CommandSyntax / Key OptionsNotes
create_clock-name clk -period 10 -waveform {0 5} [get_ports CLK]Primary clock; period in ns; waveform = {rise fall}
create_generated_clock-name clk_div2 -source [get_ports CLK] -divide_by 2 [get_pins U_DIV/Q]Derived clock; use -multiply_by for PLL
set_clock_uncertainty-setup 0.2 -hold 0.1 [get_clocks clk]Accounts for jitter + skew; applied to both edges
set_clock_latency-source 1.5 [get_clocks clk]Network delay from source to flip-flop; -source = insertion delay
set_clock_transition0.1 [get_clocks clk]Rise/fall time of clock; affects hold analysis
📥📤 IO Delays
CommandSyntaxFormula
set_input_delay-max 3.0 -clock clk [get_ports DIN]Required: (period − input_delay) available for internal logic
set_input_delay-min 0.5 -clock clk [get_ports DIN]Min = hold analysis; prevents hold violation at input FF
set_output_delay-max 2.0 -clock clk [get_ports DOUT]Time external device needs data before clock edge
set_output_delay-min -0.5 -clock clk [get_ports DOUT]Negative min = relax hold at output (data arrives before edge)
🔀 Path Exceptions
CommandKey OptionsUse When
set_multicycle_path-setup N -from FF_A -to FF_BLogic takes N cycles; always add -hold (N-1) too
set_false_path-from [get_clocks clk_a] -to [get_clocks clk_b]Async crossing, test-mode paths, non-functional paths
set_clock_groups-asynchronous -group {clk_a} -group {clk_b}Between async clock domains; no timing check between groups
set_clock_groups-exclusive -group {clk_a} -group {clk_b}Mutually exclusive clocks (e.g., test vs functional)
set_max_delay5.0 -datapath_only -from A -to BLimit combinational delay; -datapath_only skips launch/capture
📊 Timing Analysis Commands
CommandPurpose
report_timing -path_type full -delay_type maxFull setup path detail; max = setup, min = hold
report_timing -slack_lesser_than 0Report all failing paths
check_timingIdentify unconstrained paths, missing clocks
report_clock_interactionShow inter-clock relationships and safety
set_timing_derate -cell_delay 1.05 -lateOCV derating: late path 5% slower (setup pessimism)
set_timing_derate -cell_delay 0.95 -earlyOCV derating: early path 5% faster (hold pessimism)
MCP Rule: For N-cycle path: set_multicycle_path -setup N AND set_multicycle_path -hold (N-1). Missing the hold constraint is the #1 MCP mistake.
Slack = Required Time − Arrival Time. Positive = timing met. Negative = violation. Setup slack uses max delay. Hold slack uses min delay.

🔑 One-Liner Interview Answers
QuestionAnswer
Difference: port vs export?Port = requester/initiator; Export = provider/target. Port.connect(export).
Difference: TLM FIFO vs analysis port?Analysis port = 1-to-N broadcast (write only). TLM FIFO = buffered put/get channel.
factory vs config_db?Factory: replace types (what to create). config_db: pass values/handles (how to configure).
sequence vs sequence_item?sequence_item = one transaction (data). sequence = series of items (stimulus generator).
|-> vs |=>?|-> overlapping: consequent starts same cycle. |=> non-overlapping: consequent starts next cycle.
2FF sync limitation?Only for single-bit, slow-changing signals. Not for buses (all bits must be captured simultaneously).
Why gray code in async FIFO?Only 1 bit changes per count — safe to sample across clock domains (no multiple-bit glitch).
MCP hold rule?set_multicycle_path -setup N MUST be paired with -hold (N-1). Forgetting hold causes real hold violations.
💡 Interview Tips
✅ Dos & Don'ts
🎯 Explain Projects
📄 Resume Tips
💬 Behavioral Prep
✅ Technical Interview — Dos & Don'ts

✅ DO These

  • Think out loud — Walk the interviewer through your reasoning, even if you're unsure. They want to see your thought process.
  • Draw timing diagrams — For any STA, CDC, or protocol question, sketch waveforms. It shows depth.
  • Ask clarifying questions — "Is this synchronous or async?" "What's the clock frequency?" shows maturity.
  • Relate to real experience — "In my project, we used 2FF synchronizer for..." connects theory to practice.
  • Admit gaps honestly — "I haven't worked with UPF directly, but I understand the concept of power domains..." is respected.
  • Use correct terminology — Say "non-overlapping implication" not "the arrow thing." Precise language signals expertise.
  • Mention trade-offs — Every design choice has one. "Gray code FIFO needs power-of-2 depth" shows you think beyond textbooks.
  • Structure long answers — "There are 3 key points here: First... Second... Third..." keeps you organized.

❌ DON'T Do These

  • Don't memorize without understanding — "Setup time is... um... the time before clock" will fall apart with follow-ups.
  • Don't say "I think" for fundamentals — Blocking vs non-blocking is not an opinion. Know it cold.
  • Don't skip the "why" — Saying "we use gray code" without explaining WHY (only 1-bit changes) is incomplete.
  • Don't panic at unknowns — "I'm not sure, but I'd approach it by..." is way better than silence.
  • Don't over-engineer answers — If asked about a 2-bit counter, don't explain a full FIFO architecture.
  • Don't badmouth previous teams — "The RTL was terrible" reflects poorly on you, not them.
  • Don't lie about experience — Interviewers WILL drill deeper. If you claim UVM expertise, expect sequence layering questions.
  • Don't forget edge cases — Reset behavior, X-propagation, empty/full conditions. Mention them proactively.
🏢 Company-Specific Tips

🔵 Intel / AMD / NVIDIA

  • Heavy focus on RTL design fundamentals — FSMs, counters, timing
  • Expect STA deep dives — OCV, CRPR, multi-corner analysis
  • Whiteboard coding: write Verilog on the spot
  • CDC questions are common — know 2FF, handshake, async FIFO cold

🔵 Qualcomm / Samsung / MediaTek

  • Strong emphasis on UVM methodology — sequences, factory, config_db
  • Assertion-based verification — SVA writing expected
  • Protocol knowledge valued — AXI, AHB, APB
  • Power-aware verification gaining importance — UPF basics help

🟣 Synopsys / Cadence (EDA)

  • Deeper focus on algorithms & data structures alongside VLSI
  • SDC constraint writing is critical
  • Expect questions on tool flows — synthesis, P&R, STA
  • Formal verification concepts are a plus

🟢 ARM / Broadcom / TI

  • Protocol expertise is key — AMBA spec knowledge expected
  • Low power design questions common — power domains, isolation
  • Mixed-signal awareness appreciated
  • Embedded perspective — how HW/SW interact
🎯 How to Explain Your Projects in Interviews

The 2-Minute Project Pitch Framework

  • Line 1 — Context: "I worked on [project name] — a [type] for [purpose] at [company/university]."
  • Line 2 — Your Role: "I was responsible for [specific area] — [2-3 key tasks]."
  • Line 3 — Technical Meat: "The main challenge was [specific problem]. I solved it by [approach + tools]."
  • Line 4 — Result: "This improved [metric] by [number] and was [taped out / silicon-validated / etc]."
Situation: "At [company], I was part of the DV team for a [28nm/7nm] [SoC/IP block]." Task: "My responsibility was [functional verification of XYZ block / CDC closure / coverage improvement]." Action: "I built a [UVM env with constrained-random stimulus / custom scoreboard / assertion library]. The key challenge was [race condition in CDC / coverage holes in corner cases / regression failures]. I debugged using [waveform analysis / assertion-based debug / log parsing scripts]." Result: "Achieved [98% code coverage / found 12 RTL bugs / reduced regression time by 40%]. The block passed [tapeout / silicon bring-up] successfully."
🔑 What Interviewers Actually Look For

✅ Highlight These

  • Bugs you found — "I discovered a CDC bug that would have caused silicon failure." This is gold.
  • Trade-offs you made — "I chose directed tests over random for this block because coverage was already 95%."
  • Tools & methodology — Mentor tool names, UVM patterns, scripting languages.
  • Collaboration — "I worked with the RTL team to get the fix implemented and verified in 2 days."
  • Scale — Number of tests, coverage numbers, regression size, IP complexity.

❌ Avoid These

  • Vague descriptions — "I did verification" tells nothing. Be specific about WHAT you verified.
  • Only textbook knowledge — "UVM has phases" is theory. "I used build phase to configure the agent topology" is experience.
  • Claiming team work as solo — Say "I contributed to" or "my part was" — interviewers can tell.
  • Ignoring failures — Mentioning bugs you MISSED (and what you learned) shows maturity.
📋 Strong Action Verbs for VLSI/DV

Use These in Your Answers

  • Designed / Architected / Developed — for creating new components
  • Debugged / Diagnosed / Root-caused — for finding issues
  • Automated / Scripted / Streamlined — for improving efficiency
  • Verified / Validated / Signed-off — for closure activities
  • Optimized / Improved / Reduced — for performance gains (always quantify!)
  • Collaborated / Coordinated / Reviewed — for teamwork
📄 Resume Tips for VLSI / DV Roles

✅ Resume Must-Haves

  • Technical Skills section — List: SystemVerilog, UVM, SVA, Verilog, Python/Perl, SDC, STA tools (PrimeTime, Tempus), simulators (VCS, Xcelium, QuestaSim)
  • Quantify everything — "Achieved 97% functional coverage" not "improved coverage"
  • Project bullet format: [Action Verb] + [What] + [How/Tool] + [Result/Impact]
  • Keep it 1 page for <5 years experience, 2 pages max for senior
  • Tailor per job description — If JD says "CDC experience required," put your CDC project FIRST
  • Include relevant coursework — Digital Design, VLSI, Computer Architecture, Verification Methodology

❌ Resume Mistakes

  • Generic objective — "Seeking a challenging role..." is wasted space. Use a 2-line summary instead.
  • Listing every tool ever — Only include tools you can discuss in depth. If you list Specman, you'd better know it.
  • No numbers — "Responsible for verification" vs "Verified 15+ RTL modules, found 23 bugs, achieved 98% coverage"
  • Typos in technical terms — "System Verilog" (wrong) vs "SystemVerilog" (correct). Details matter in DV!
  • Hiding gaps — Brief career gaps are normal. Don't fake dates.
  • PDF only — Some ATS systems can't parse fancy PDFs. Have a clean, simple version ready.
📝 Resume Bullet Templates
DV Engineer Bullet Examples: • Developed UVM-based verification environment for [block name] including driver, monitor, scoreboard, and coverage model; achieved 98% code coverage and 95% functional coverage across 500+ test scenarios. • Identified and root-caused 15+ RTL bugs through constrained-random testing and assertion-based verification using SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA). • Automated regression infrastructure using Python scripts, reducing nightly regression runtime from 8 hours to 3 hours (62% improvement). • Performed CDC analysis using [Spyglass/Meridian] and implemented 2FF synchronizers and handshake protocols for 12 clock domain crossings. • Wrote SDC constraints including create_clock, set_false_path, and set_multicycle_path; achieved timing closure at [frequency] on [node].
🎯 ATS-Friendly Keywords

Include These Keywords (If Applicable)

  • Languages: SystemVerilog, Verilog, VHDL, SVA, UPF, SDC, TCL, Python, Perl, C/C++
  • Methodologies: UVM, OVM, VMM, ABV, Formal Verification, Emulation, FPGA Prototyping
  • Tools: VCS, Xcelium, QuestaSim, PrimeTime, Tempus, ICC2, Innovus, Spyglass, JasperGold, Verdi, DVE
  • Concepts: CDC, STA, DFT, Low Power, AMBA/AXI, Coverage-Driven Verification, Constrained Random
  • Flows: RTL-to-GDS, Synthesis, Place & Route, Timing Closure, ECO, Tapeout, Silicon Bring-up
💬 Behavioral Interview Preparation

🌟 STAR Method — Your Answer Framework

  • S — Situation: Set the scene. What project? What team? What was happening?
  • T — Task: What was YOUR specific responsibility or challenge?
  • A — Action: What did YOU do? (Be specific — tools, steps, decisions)
  • R — Result: What was the outcome? (Quantify: bugs found, time saved, coverage achieved)
📋 Top 10 Behavioral Questions for DV Engineers

1. "Tell me about a critical bug you found late in the project."

"At [company], during final regression on a 7nm SoC, I found a CDC bug in the power controller — a multi-bit bus was crossing domains without synchronization. I used Spyglass CDC to trace it, wrote a directed test to reproduce it, and worked with RTL to add a gray-coded handshake. This would have been a silicon respin — saving approximately $2M."

2. "Describe a time you disagreed with a team member."

"The RTL designer wanted to skip CDC analysis for an 'almost synchronous' interface. I demonstrated with a waveform that a 10ppm frequency difference could cause metastability within 1 hour of operation. We added a FIFO synchronizer — and it caught an actual issue in silicon validation."

3. "How do you handle tight deadlines?"

"During tapeout crunch, we had 200+ timing violations in 3 days. I triaged by severity — fixed hold violations first (irreversible in silicon), then setup violations. I automated ECO buffer insertion with a TCL script, closing 80% of violations automatically. We taped out on schedule."

4. "Tell me about a time you had to learn something quickly."

"I was assigned UPF-based power-aware verification with no prior experience. I spent a weekend studying UPF syntax, then built a minimal power-aware testbench. Within 2 weeks, I found 3 isolation cell bugs that the non-PA simulation missed. I documented my learnings as a team wiki."

5. "Describe your debugging approach."

"I follow a systematic method: (1) Reproduce with minimal test. (2) Narrow scope — is it RTL, TB, or assertion? (3) Add targeted assertions around the failure point. (4) Binary search on stimulus to isolate trigger. (5) Root-cause and verify fix doesn't break existing tests."

6. "How do you prioritize when everything is urgent?"

"I categorize by impact: (1) Silicon-critical bugs first (CDC, reset). (2) Functional correctness. (3) Coverage closure. (4) Code quality. I communicate priorities to the lead daily and adjust based on tapeout milestones."

7. "Tell me about a project you're most proud of."

"Building the UVM environment for a DDR PHY controller from scratch. I designed the sequence library, constrained-random stimulus, and a self-checking scoreboard. The env found 28 RTL bugs in the first regression run and became the team's reference implementation for future projects."

8. "How do you ensure quality in your work?"

"Three layers: (1) Self-review — I re-read my code after 24 hours with fresh eyes. (2) Coverage analysis — I check what my tests DON'T cover. (3) Peer review — I actively request code reviews and incorporate feedback before merging."

9. "Describe a situation where you improved a process."

"Our regression took 12 hours nightly. I profiled the testbench and found 30% of time was in unused coverage sampling. I added coverage pragma guards and parallelized independent test groups. Runtime dropped to 4.5 hours — a 62% improvement."

10. "Where do you see yourself in 5 years?"

"I want to grow into a senior verification engineer / lead role. Specifically, I'm interested in [formal verification / emulation / architecture-level verification]. I want to influence verification strategy at the block-to-SoC level and mentor junior engineers."
